title: On Women's Right to Vote: argument, inference and evidence
prompt: Read the excerpt, then choose the best answer for each question.

choices.text: By voting she committed no crime; she used a citizen's right the Constitution guarantees
She regrets voting and asks the audience to forgive her
choices.misconception: misses her claim that she "committed no crime"

choices.text: Governments have the power to give women rights
choices.misconception: takes the "old dogma" she rejects as her claim

choices.text: Women should be allowed to run for President
choices.misconception: names a claim she never makes; she argues only about voting

items.stem: What can you infer about why Anthony quotes the Declaration of Independence at length?

choices.text: She disagrees with it and wants it changed
choices.misconception: contradicts her use of it as proof

choices.text: She expects her audience to accept it as an authority, so its words strengthen her case
She wants to show it names women directly
choices.misconception: overlooks that the quoted words say "all men"

choices.text: She is filling time before her real point
choices.misconception: infers a motive that no detail supports

items.stem: According to Anthony, what do people agree to when they form a free government?

choices.text: To give their natural rights to the government
choices.misconception: overlooks that they "do not barter away their natural rights"

choices.text: To let the strongest person settle disputes
choices.misconception: reverses "abandon the methods of brute force"

choices.text: To vote in every election
choices.misconception: draws a conclusion about voting that this paragraph does not state

choices.text: To protect each other's rights through courts and lawmakers instead of force

items.stem: Which evidence does Anthony use to support her claim?

choices.text: The verdict of her own trial
choices.misconception: names a verdict as evidence, though she is still only charged

choices.text: Figures on how many women voted
choices.misconception: names statistics, a kind of evidence the speech never uses

choices.text: The Declaration of Independence's words that governments get "their just powers from the consent of the governed"
Her own feelings about the election
choices.misconception: takes her personal situation for her evidence, not the documents

items.stem: Which two details together show that Anthony believes rights come before government?

choices.text: "Before governments were organized... each individual possessed the right" and "I stand before you to-night, under indictment"
choices.misconception: pairs a strong detail with one about her own situation

choices.text: "Before governments were organized... each individual possessed the right to protect his own life" and "Not one of them pretends to bestow rights."
"They agree to abandon the methods of brute force" and "It shall be my work this evening to prove to you"
choices.misconception: picks details about methods and her plan, not where rights come from

choices.text: "Not one of them pretends to bestow rights" and "Friends and Fellow-citizens"
choices.misconception: pairs a strong detail with her greeting, which supports nothing

items.stem: Anthony says she will prove that she "simply exercised" her citizen's right. What does "simply" suggest about how she sees her act?

choices.text: She admits voting was easy but wrong
choices.misconception: reads "simply" as an admission, missing "committed no crime"

choices.text: She sees voting as an ordinary act of a citizen, not a bold crime
She means she voted only once
choices.misconception: takes "simply" as a count instead of a judgment of the act

choices.text: She thinks voting is unimportant
choices.misconception: infers indifference, though she builds a whole speech on it

items.stem: Anthony asks how "the consent of the governed" can be given "if the right to vote be denied." What reasoning does this question show?

choices.text: If government rests on the consent of the governed, denying the vote denies people a way to consent
Voting matters less than consent
choices.misconception: misses that she treats the vote as the way consent is given

choices.text: The Declaration is out of date
choices.misconception: misjudges her reasoning; she relies on the Declaration as authority

choices.text: Women never agreed to the Declaration
choices.misconception: mistakes her reasoning about voting for a claim about the Declaration

items.stem: Which two details together show that Anthony believes government exists to protect rights?

choices.text: "We assert the province of government to be to secure the people in the enjoyment of their unalienable rights" and "I stand before you to-night, under indictment"
choices.misconception: pairs a strong detail with one about her own situation

choices.text: "Friends and Fellow-citizens" and "It shall be my work this evening to prove to you"
choices.misconception: picks her greeting and her plan, neither about government's purpose

choices.text: "We assert the province of government to be to secure the people in the enjoyment of their unalienable rights" and "That to secure these, governments are instituted among men"
"They agree to abandon the methods of brute force" and "the alleged crime of having voted"
choices.misconception: picks details about settling disputes and her charge, not government's purpose

items.stem: Why does Anthony add the Quaker preacher's words, "of all women"?

choices.text: To show that the Declaration's "all men" should include women too
To show that Quakers wrote the Declaration
choices.misconception: draws a conclusion about authorship the text doesn't support

choices.text: To show that only women have the right to vote
choices.misconception: overlooks "of all men" just before "of all women"

choices.text: To make the audience laugh
choices.misconception: infers a joke with no support in the passage

items.stem: Anthony says the founding documents "propose to protect the people" and "Not one of them pretends to bestow rights." Why is this point relevant to her argument?

choices.text: It proves the Constitution names women's right to vote
choices.misconception: overstates the evidence; she never shows women named in it

choices.text: It is not relevant; it only reviews history
choices.misconception: misses how the point connects to her claim about voting

choices.text: It shows that government should create new rights for women
choices.misconception: reverses her reasoning that governments do not give rights

choices.text: If government does not create rights, a state cannot take away the vote citizens already have
